A curatorial statement and exhibition provocation for Toronto, Canada, addressing the need to reimagine our relationships with the world around us — critiquing modern abstractions and linear narratives while questioning how communities might move forward differently. The exhibition features six Canadian and South Korean artists whose practices examine tangles of organic, mechanical, and artificial intelligences, developed through collaborative field studies at a regenerative farm in Quebec.

title: Cultural Fermentation: on Craft, Ecology, Listening, and Safety
subtitle: Workshop abstract — Culture x AI Workshop, Doing AI Differently, ICML 2026
excerpt: Arts and cultural programming constitute core safety infrastructure — the generative prior condition without which governance cannot take root in communities — rather than a supplement to technical governance.
body:
Presented July 10–11, 2026 at the Doing AI Differently Culture x AI Workshop, held alongside the International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) in Seoul, South Korea.

**Abstract:** Conversations around AI safety tend to centre on regulatory frameworks, technical specifications, and institutional compliance. Through the perspective of arts and cultural production, we argue that we urgently need approaches centred on developing public imagination and localized capacity to steward AI infrastructures and generate shared knowledge. Drawing on Soetsu Yanagi's Mingei philosophy, Lambert Zuidervaart's concept of imaginative disclosure, and ecological models of intelligence developed through arts practices, Cultural Fermentation proposes that arts and cultural programming constitute core safety infrastructure — the generative prior condition without which governance cannot take root in communities — rather than as a supplement to technical governance.

A three-year cross-disciplinary program exploring how AI and technology can deepen ecological engagement rather than perpetuate extraction. The initiative examines the colonial legacies embedded in mapping and data systems while investigating alternative technological approaches to environmental and cultural restoration. "Just as we inhabit our physical bodies, we inhabit landscapes and live within and from them."
